activities.anchor: creeping over the hot, yielding rock beneath
activities.caption: place the plates' pace on the scale
activities.name: ocPlatePlace

config.prompt: Earth's plates creep along at "a few centimetres per year" — about the rate your fingernails grow. Place that speed:
config.why: A few centimetres per year — fingernail speed. Almost all the planet's earthquakes and volcanoes are concentrated where the plates meet.

activities.anchor: The clinching evidence, assembled in the 1960s
activities.caption: rebuild the spreading argument, step by step
activities.name: ocSpreadingOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the three-line argument that proved seafloor spreading:
items: Rock cools at the ridge, magnetised in the direction of Earth's field at that moment
The crust spreads away, so stripes of alternating magnetisation run symmetrically either side of every ridge
Core samples show the stripes are oldest farthest from the ridge
Earthquake foci trace the slabs diving back down at the trenches — subduction recycles the crust
Result: no seafloor older than about 200 million years survives, against continents nearly 4 billion
config.why: A bar-code of creation — and the Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep, about 11 km) is subduction's leftover.

activities.anchor: narrow off tectonically active coasts like California
activities.caption: pair each margin feature with its character
activities.name: ocMarginMatch

config.prompt: The continental margin and beyond — pair each feature with its signature:

pairs.right: gently sloping underwater extension of the continent — shallow enough for light and nutrients, the ocean's richest fishing ground
the drop from shelf toward the deep
built of sediments carried off the shelf by gravity flows
the largest single habitat type on Earth — flat under fine sediment raining down for millions of years
the longest mountain chain on the planet, some 65,000 km, mostly submarine

config.why: The shelf is narrow off tectonically active coasts and hundreds of kilometres wide off passive margins like Argentina.

activities.anchor: sea level itself is not fixed
activities.caption: file each mover by its scope
activities.name: ocSeaBuckets

config.prompt: Sea level is always a two-number story — file each cause:
buckets: local — the land or the coast itself

items.label: ice ages lock water into continental sheets — at the last glacial maximum sea level stood roughly 120–130 m lower, exposing Beringia and Sunda
high ridge activity — the spreading ridges' swollen volume displaces water
land rebounds after ice sheets melt
land sinks where sediments compact or groundwater is pumped out (Bangkok, Jakarta)

config.why: This is why tide gauges must be pinned to bedrock to mean anything — the ocean rising and the land moving are different numbers.

config.prompt: The Sun's pull on Earth is roughly 180 times the Moon's — yet it raises smaller bulges. Its tide-raising force is about what multiple of the Moon's?
config.why: About 0.46 — tide-raising force falls with the cube of distance, and the Sun is 400 times farther away. The Moon, small and near, rules the tides.
config.context: At new and full moon the solar and lunar bulges align (spring tides); at quarter moon they fight (neap tides).

activities.anchor: Water in a basin rocks like water in a bath
activities.caption: true or false — basin resonance
activities.name: ocResonanceJudge

statements.s: Basin water has a natural rocking period set by the basin's depth and length.
statements.why: Resonant basin oscillations — the real ocean's response, on top of the equilibrium bulges.

statements.s: Where the natural period matches the tidal forcing, the tide is amplified enormously.
statements.why: The Bay of Fundy's 12–16 m range is the classic case.

statements.s: The equilibrium-bulge theory alone correctly predicts which coasts get one tide a day.
statements.why: Bulge theory gives everyone two — basin geometry is why much of the Gulf of Mexico gets one (diurnal) and some coasts almost none.

statements.s: Real tides are sums of dozens of constituents, each written as a sinusoid.
statements.why: Astronomical rhythms added together — which is why tides are predictable.

activities.anchor: tide prediction is harmonic analysis with a maritime purpose
activities.caption: fill the two constituent periods
activities.name: ocClockCloze

config.text: The fast ripple on the tide plot is the %%0%%-hour lunar semidiurnal constituent; the slow drift is the %%1%%-hour diurnal constituent, which makes one of each day's two high tides taller — a mixed tide, the daily inequality visible along much of the US Pacific coast.
config.hint: The Moon advances on its orbit as Earth spins — and the slower clock runs about a solar day.

activities.caption: pair each pelagic zone with its band
activities.name: ocZonesMatch

config.prompt: The water column, top to bottom — pair each zone with its depth band and its rule for life:

pairs.right: 0–200 m — enough light for photosynthesis, the ocean's farmland and most of its familiar life
200–1,000 m — light dwindles to nothing; fish here run the daily vertical migration, the largest animal migration on Earth
1,000–4,000 m — midnight black, about 2–4 °C, fed by the snow of organic debris from above
4,000–6,000 m — the abyssal plains' water column
below 6,000 m — the trenches' own realm

config.why: Pressure climbs one atmosphere every ten metres — each zone is really a different planet with different rules for life.
